issues.legal_issue: Information disclosing a cognizable offence must be registered without first assessing its reliability or credibility.
material_facts: The complainant submitted information to the police alleging a cognizable offence, but the police did not register a case.
The High Court declined to direct registration, referring to a pending contempt petition and an alternative remedy.
The court did not decide the merits of the underlying allegations.
issues.conclusion: The police were required to register a case because the information disclosed a cognizable offence; its genuineness or credibility could be considered only after registration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes registration mandatory when information laid before the officer in charge discloses a cognizable offence. Reliability or credibility is not a condition precedent. The court relied on State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, [1992] Supp. 1 SCC 335, particularly paragraphs 31–33, which also explain the statutory route under Section 154(3) when an officer refuses to register a case. The availability of an alternative remedy or pendency of contempt proceedings does not substitute for the registration duty.

rule.if: criminal_information_about_cognizable_offence and information_discloses_cognizable_offence and police_received_information and police_refused_registration

predicates.criminal_information_about_cognizable_of: The matter involves information given to the police reporting a criminal offence.
predicates.information_discloses_cognizable_offence: The information describes facts that disclose a cognizable offence.
predicates.police_received_information: The police received the information reporting the alleged offence.
predicates.police_refused_registration: The police did not register a case on the basis of the information.

issues.definition: When information reporting a criminal offence is received by police, discloses a cognizable offence, and is not registered, the police must register a case.

issues.legal_issue: An independent agency should register and investigate a complaint alleging wrongdoing by police personnel when independent investigation better serves the interests of justice.
material_facts: The complaint was against a police officer and had not resulted in registration of a case by the local police.
The parties did not dispute that the interests of justice would be better served by directing the Central Bureau of Investigation to register and investigate the case.
The Additional Solicitor General accepted that the Central Bureau of Investigation would be an appropriate authority if registration and investigation were directed.
issues.conclusion: The court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation to register a case on the complaint and investigate it.
issues.legal_principle: Where allegations are made against police personnel, the interests of justice may be better served by registration and investigation by an independent agency. Applying that principle to the circumstances and the parties’ positions, the court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation to act.

predicates.criminal_complaint: The proceeding concerns a complaint reporting alleged criminal conduct.
predicates.complaint_alleges_police_misconduct: The complaint alleges wrongdoing by police personnel.
predicates.local_police_failed_to_register_case: The local police did not register a case on the complaint.

issues.definition: When a criminal complaint alleges police misconduct and the local police have not registered a case, an independent agency must register and investigate the case.
